## Why CUDA Graph Replay Can Be Faster

When you launch kernels eagerly (one `cudaLaunchKernel` call at a time), each launch involves a round-trip through the CUDA driver: the host-side API call validates parameters, allocates or retrieves a launch configuration, and enqueues the work onto the GPU's command queue. This per-launch overhead—typically on the order of several microseconds—adds up quickly when you have hundreds or thousands of small kernels. The GPU may also experience gaps between kernels while the CPU is still preparing the next launch, leading to underutilization of the hardware.

A CUDA graph captures the entire sequence of kernel launches, their dependencies, and their parameters into a single immutable structure. When you **replay** that graph, the driver submits the whole thing as one operation. The GPU's scheduler can then walk the pre-validated dependency graph internally, launching kernels back-to-back with minimal inter-kernel latency. Because the launch metadata is already resolved, the driver skips most of the per-launch validation and setup work.
